name: Buxa
tagline: A Bhutanese fort and prison in the clouds above the Dooars
summary: Buxa Tiger Reserve climbs from the plains near Alipurduar to the Bhutan border, and on its slopes stands Buxa Fort, once Bhutanese, then a British prison. Allow two nights for the fort walk, Jayanti and a jungle drive.
meta_description: Buxa guide: the Buxa Fort walk from Santalabari, Lepchakha, Jayanti and Rajabhatkhawa, homestays, costs and park closure from 16 June to 15 September.
intro: Buxa Tiger Reserve covers about 760 km² of Alipurduar district, rising from about 60 m on the plains to 1,750 m on the Bhutan border. It was set up in 1983 as one of India's early tiger reserves, and its forests link with Bhutan's Phibsoo sanctuary and with Manas in Assam. Tigers are now very rarely seen, but elephants, gaur, leopards, clouded leopards and more than 280 bird species live here.

The reserve's gateway is Rajabhatkhawa, about 17 km from Alipurduar, with an entry gate and a nature interpretation centre. From there one road leads through forest to Santalabari, the start of the walk to Buxa Fort at 867 m, and another to Jayanti, a village on a wide river below the hills.

Buxa Fort was a Bhutanese fort guarding one of the passes, or duars, into Bhutan. The British took it in 1865 and later used it as a high-security prison for Indian freedom fighters. After 1959 it sheltered Tibetan monks who had fled to India. Today it is a quiet ruin above forest and villages, with views over the plains.

highlights.title: Buxa Fort walk
highlights.text: A forest path of about 4–5 km from Santalabari climbs to the fort ruins and the village of Buxa.

highlights.title: Lepchakha
highlights.text: A Drukpa village about 5 km above the fort, on a ridge with wide views over the Dooars rivers.

highlights.title: Jayanti river
highlights.text: A broad stony river at the foot of the hills, with walks towards the Mahakal caves.

highlights.title: Rajabhatkhawa
highlights.text: The reserve's gateway, with a nature interpretation centre and forest drives.

highlights.title: Birds and butterflies
highlights.text: Hornbills, forest birds and many butterflies on the lower slopes.

facts: 17 km to Rajabhatkhawa, 32 km to Santalabari
Reserve tourism closed 16 June to 15 September
None; reserve entry and guide fees apply

how_to_reach.text: Take a bus or train to Alipurduar, then a local bus or shared jeep to Rajabhatkhawa and on to Santalabari or Jayanti; services are irregular, so start early.
A reserved car from Siliguri takes 4.5–5 hours to Rajabhatkhawa (about 175 km) and costs ₹5,000–6,500; from Madarihat it is about 1.5 hours.
Alipurduar Junction and New Alipurduar are the nearest major stations, about 20–25 km from Rajabhatkhawa.

where_to_stay: Simple family homestays in Santalabari, Buxa village and Lepchakha cost about ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals, though rules on homestays inside the reserve have tightened and some have closed. Jayanti and Rajabhatkhawa have a few lodges and forest department accommodation. Alipurduar town, 17 km away, has hotels at all prices and makes an easy base.
tips: Start the Buxa Fort walk by mid-morning so you are back before dusk, or stay a night in the village.
Take a guide from the counter at Santalabari; it is required and helps the village economy.
Wear proper walking shoes; the path is stony and slippery after rain.
Carry cash; there are no ATMs beyond Alipurduar.
Homestay rules inside the reserve change often. Check current status before you travel.

local_word.meaning: Door or gate. The Dooars are named after the duars, the passes into Bhutan, and Buxa guarded one of them.

story.title: From Bhutanese fort to prison in the clouds
paras: Buxa Fort stands at 867 m on a forested spur above the plains. It was first a Bhutanese fort, built to command the Buxa Duar, one of the passes that linked the Bengal plains with Bhutan. Whoever held the duars controlled trade, and taxes, between the hills and the lowlands.

In the Duar War of 1864–65, British Indian forces occupied Buxa as part of their campaign to take the Bengal Duars. The Treaty of Sinchula, signed on 11 November 1865, confirmed British possession of the Bengal and Assam Duars, and the British rebuilt the fort in stone.

Remote and hard to reach, the fort became a high-security prison. It operated as a special jail from 1942 to 1947 and again from 1949 to 1951, holding political prisoners including revolutionaries from groups such as Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar. The Bengali poet Subhash Mukhopadhyay was held here and wrote of it as a prison in the clouds.

After the Tibetan uprising of March 1959, hundreds of monks fled to India, many from Drepung Monastery. They set up a monastic study centre and refugee camp at the old fort, known as Buxa Chogar, and lived and studied there until they were moved to Karnataka in 1971. Today a few walls, a memorial and the village remain.

faqs.q: How long is the Buxa Fort walk?
faqs.a: From Santalabari the path to Buxa Fort is about 4–5 km one way, with roughly 2.5 km of easy forest walking and then a steady climb. Most people take 1.5–2 hours up and a little less down. Continuing to Lepchakha adds about 5 km more. It is a moderate walk for anyone reasonably fit.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: Yes. A local guide is required for the walk and is arranged at the counter where the path begins in Santalabari. The fee is modest and goes to the village. Guides know the path, the history and the local homestays, and they can arrange porters.

faqs.q: Can I see tigers at Buxa?
faqs.a: It is very unlikely. Buxa was declared a tiger reserve in 1983, but tiger numbers have been very low for many years and sightings are rare. Come for the forest, the walk, birds, butterflies and the history of the fort, and treat any big cat sighting as extraordinary luck.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: Yes, in simple homestays in Buxa village beside the fort or in Lepchakha above it, though which homestays may operate inside the reserve has changed after court and forest department orders. Ask at Santalabari or Alipurduar. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is Lepchakha?
faqs.a: Lepchakha is a small Drukpa village about 5 km beyond Buxa Fort, on a ridge at the edge of the Bhutan hills. From its open ground you look down over the plains and the braided channels of the Dooars rivers. It makes a good overnight stop or a longer day walk from Santalabari.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Buxa?
faqs.a: November to April is best, with dry paths and clear views. December and January mornings are foggy and cold at the fort. The reserve closes for tourism from 16 June to 15 September, and monsoon rain makes the path slippery and rivers dangerous.

faqs.q: How do I get to Buxa from Siliguri?
faqs.a: Drive about 175 km to Rajabhatkhawa (4.5–5 hours), then 15 km to Santalabari. Or take a train or bus to Alipurduar and a car from there. Many travellers combine Buxa with Jaldapara and Chilapata, which are 1–2 hours away.

faqs.q: What is Jayanti?
faqs.a: Jayanti is a village on the wide, stony bed of the Jayanti river at the foot of the Bhutan hills, about 13 km from Rajabhatkhawa. It has views of forest-covered hills, walks along the river, and a path towards the Mahakal caves. After rain the river can flood quickly, so take local advice.

faqs.q: Is Buxa suitable for families?
faqs.a: Families with children who enjoy walking will love the fort walk and village stays. Very young children or older relatives may prefer to stay at Rajabhatkhawa or Alipurduar and visit Jayanti and the interpretation centre by car. The path has no railings in places, so keep children close.

experiences.title: Walk up to Buxa Fort from Santalabari
experiences.summary: A guided forest walk of about 4–5 km each way from Santalabari to the ruins of Buxa Fort and the village beside it.
body: The path starts at Santalabari, where you register and take a guide. The first part runs gently through forest; then the path climbs steadily on stone steps and earth, through sal, bamboo and mixed woods full of butterflies and birds. Porters carry supplies up the same path to the village.

At the top are the fort's remaining walls, a memorial to the freedom fighters held here, and the small village of Buxa with its homestays and tea stalls. Return the same way, or stay a night and continue to Lepchakha next morning.
experiences.best_time: Start by 9 am between November and April.
experiences.cost: ₹500–1,000 guide fee per group, plus reserve entry (indicative)

faqs.q: How hard is the Buxa Fort walk?
faqs.a: It is moderate. The distance is about 4–5 km each way with a climb of several hundred metres, mostly on a clear path with steps. Anyone who can walk uphill for an hour and a half with rests can manage. Wear good shoes; the stones are slippery when wet.

faqs.q: What is there to see at Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: Parts of the old stone walls and buildings, a memorial to the political prisoners held here, the village of Buxa, and views over forest to the plains on clear days. Do not expect a complete fort; it is a ruin among trees.

faqs.q: Can I walk to Buxa Fort without staying overnight?
faqs.a: Yes. Most day visitors start from Santalabari by mid-morning, spend an hour at the top and walk down by mid-afternoon. Allow 4–5 hours in all. Drive from Alipurduar, Rajabhatkhawa or Jayanti on the same day.

experiences.title: Ridge walk to Lepchakha
experiences.duration: 3–4 hours from Buxa Fort and back
experiences.summary: A walk of about 5 km beyond Buxa Fort to the Drukpa village of Lepchakha, with wide views over the plains and rivers of the Dooars.
body: From Buxa village the path continues uphill through forest and small fields to Lepchakha, a village of Drukpa families on a ridge facing south. The last part opens up on to grassy ground where on a clear day you can see the rivers of the Dooars spreading over the plains below.

The village has a small Buddhist shrine and a few homestays. Ask before entering homes or the shrine and keep your voice low. Sunrise and sunset from Lepchakha are worth an overnight stay if homestays are open.
experiences.best_time: Clear days from November to February; set out early before haze builds.
experiences.cost: ₹500–1,000 guide fee per group (indicative); homestays extra

faqs.q: How far is Lepchakha from Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: About 5 km, a walk of 1.5–2 hours each way with some steep sections. From Santalabari to Lepchakha the total is about 9–10 km. Many people walk to the fort on day one, stay the night and go to Lepchakha the next morning.

faqs.q: Who lives in Lepchakha?
faqs.a: Lepchakha is a small Drukpa village, people with close ties to Bhutan, who are mostly Buddhist. Families farm, keep animals and run a few homestays. Treat the shrine and homes with respect, and ask before photographing people.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Lepchakha?
faqs.a: A few family homestays have hosted walkers, but rules on homestays inside Buxa Tiger Reserve have changed in recent years. Ask your guide at Santalabari what is open. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Jayanti riverbed and the path to Mahakal
experiences.summary: A walk on the wide bed of the Jayanti river below the Bhutan hills, with a longer guided option towards the Mahakal caves.
body: Jayanti village sits beside a broad, stony river that comes out of the hills and spreads over the plain. In the dry season you can walk on the riverbed with forest on both sides and the hills ahead. It is a fine place for a quiet morning, birds and photographs.

With a local guide you can follow the river and then a steep path up to the Mahakal caves, limestone caves held sacred by local Hindus, which make a half-day outing. The path crosses water and rocks and is not suitable after rain. Do not go alone; ask in Jayanti about the current state of the path.
experiences.best_time: Mornings from November to March, when the river is low.
experiences.cost: ₹0 for the riverbed; ₹500–1,000 for a Mahakal guide (indicative)

faqs.q: How far is Jayanti from Rajabhatkhawa?
faqs.a: About 13 km through the forest of Buxa Tiger Reserve, roughly 30–40 minutes by car. Pay the reserve entry fee at Rajabhatkhawa. From Alipurduar it is about 30 km. Local jeeps run from Alipurduar and Rajabhatkhawa at irregular times.

faqs.q: Is the Mahakal cave walk difficult?
faqs.a: It is moderately hard: a walk along the river and over stones, then a steep climb. Allow half a day with a local guide. Do not attempt it after heavy rain, when the river rises fast. Wear shoes with grip and carry water.

faqs.q: Can I swim in the Jayanti river?
faqs.a: It is not advised. The river is shallow for much of the dry season but has fast channels, and floods can come suddenly after rain in the Bhutan hills. Paddling at the edge with others nearby is fine in winter.

experiences.title: Forest drive from Rajabhatkhawa
experiences.summary: A drive through the forest of Buxa Tiger Reserve from Rajabhatkhawa, with a stop at the nature interpretation centre, for elephants, gaur and birds.
body: Rajabhatkhawa is the main entry to Buxa Tiger Reserve. Its nature interpretation centre explains the reserve's forests and animals. From the gate, forest roads run towards Jayanti and Santalabari through sal and mixed forest, and a jungle drive in an open jeep gives you a chance of elephants, gaur, deer and many birds.

Local people say the name Rajabhatkhawa means the place where the king ate rice, and tell of a meal shared here by a king of Cooch Behar and a Bhutanese ruler. We have not found a written source for the tale. Drives and routes are set by the forest department and change from season to season.
experiences.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon between November and April.
experiences.cost: ₹2,000–3,000 per jeep with entry and guide (indicative)

faqs.q: What can I see on a Buxa jungle drive?
faqs.a: Elephants, gaur, sambar, barking deer, wild boar and many birds, including hornbills, are possible. Leopards and other cats are seldom seen. The forest is dense, so sightings are less certain than at Jaldapara, but there are far fewer vehicles.

faqs.q: How do I book a Buxa jungle drive?
faqs.a: Ask at the forest office and counter at Rajabhatkhawa, or through your lodge in Rajabhatkhawa, Jayanti or Alipurduar. Routes and fees are set by the forest department and change. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What does Rajabhatkhawa mean?
faqs.a: In Bengali it is usually read as the place where the king ate rice. Locals tell a story of a king of Cooch Behar sharing a meal here with a Bhutanese ruler to settle a dispute. It is a local tradition; we have not found a written record of the event.
